prompt: Match each provider to its usual unit of isolation.
hint: The container that holds resources and carries a bill.

prompt: A Google Cloud administrator grants `roles/storage.objectViewer` to a group on a folder. Which buckets can the group now read?
hint: Grants at Google Cloud flow down.

choices.text: None until each bucket also names the group
choices.why: That would be AWS's habit; at Google Cloud the folder's grant already reaches the buckets below.

choices.text: Every bucket in every project under the folder, including future ones
choices.why: Right. A grant made high up is a grant on everything below it.

choices.text: Only buckets created by members of that group
choices.why: Who created a bucket plays no part in the allow policy.

choices.text: The buckets in the folder's first project, since a binding attaches to exactly one project
choices.why: A binding on a folder applies to every project in it.

prompt: Where do the identities that act on an Azure subscription live?
hint: A subscription is where they are given roles.

choices.text: In the tenant's directory, Microsoft Entra ID
choices.why: Right. Who can touch a subscription starts with a directory that serves every other one too.

choices.text: In the subscription itself, one directory per subscription
choices.why: That is closer to an AWS account's IAM. Azure subscriptions hold no identities of their own.

choices.text: In each resource group
choices.why: A resource group is a scope for role assignments, not a directory.

choices.text: In Azure Policy, beside the guardrails that govern the subscription
choices.why: Azure Policy governs configuration; it holds no identities.

prompt: The clinic attaches an SCP denying `s3:PutBucketPublicAccessBlock` to its organisation's root, and runs its workloads in the management account. What does the SCP do to those workloads?
hint: One account is outside every SCP.

choices.text: It protects them, because an SCP on the root covers every account
choices.why: Every account except the management account, which is exactly where the workloads are.

choices.text: It blocks every S3 request made from the management account
choices.why: It names one action, and even that does not reach the management account.

choices.text: Nothing at all; that account is exempt
choices.why: Right: an SCP never applies to the management account, which is why it should hold no workloads.

choices.text: It grants them the permission to change the switches
choices.why: An SCP grants nothing; it only limits.

prompt: Match each provider to the mechanism that puts a guardrail on a whole branch of its hierarchy.
hint: The last row of the first table.

pairs.right: Azure Policy with a Deny effect

prompt: A Google Cloud bucket grants `roles/storage.objectViewer` to `allAuthenticatedUsers`. Who can read it?
hint: Authenticated never means ours.

choices.text: Members of the clinic's organisation
choices.why: That is the misreading the lesson warns about.

choices.text: Its project's service accounts
choices.why: Nothing about the name limits it to a project, or to service accounts.

choices.text: Nobody until a deny policy is removed
choices.why: No deny policy is involved; the binding grants.

choices.text: Anybody signed in to any Google account
choices.why: Right. Every Google account on the planet.

prompt: A reviewer wants to stop one person deleting storage on Azure, the way an explicit Deny would on AWS. What does the lesson say is the usual Azure way?
hint: Azure RBAC is additive.

choices.text: Write a deny assignment for that person
choices.why: Customers do not write deny assignments freely; Azure creates them for features such as managed applications.

choices.text: Add a second role assignment with fewer permissions, so the narrower one wins
choices.why: A second grant adds to the first; it never subtracts.

choices.text: Take away the grant, or refuse the change with Azure Policy
choices.why: Right. Permissions are the union of grants, so you take grants away; a policy constrains the resource.

choices.text: Move the person to another tenant
choices.why: Far beyond what the problem needs, and not what the lesson describes.

prompt: An Azure access review lists every Owner and User Access Administrator on every subscription and finds three people. Who has it missed?
hint: Two planes meet at one documented switch.

choices.text: Nobody: subscription roles are the only way to administer Azure resources
choices.why: The directory's top role can elevate itself into them.

choices.text: Anyone with Reader on a resource group
choices.why: Reader reads; it cannot grant.

choices.text: The managed identities of virtual machines, which inherit Owner from the subscription
choices.why: A managed identity has the roles assigned to it and nothing inherited by default.

choices.text: Global Administrators in Entra ID, through elevate access
choices.why: Right. An Azure owner in waiting, invisible to an RBAC-only review.

prompt: Which Google Cloud Organization Policy constraint does the lesson name for refusing long-lived secrets for programs?
hint: Service account keys.

choices.text: `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation`
choices.why: Right. It refuses creating service account keys across a folder or organisation.

choices.text: `storage.publicAccessPrevention`
choices.why: That one refuses public buckets.

choices.text: `compute.skipDefaultNetworkCreation`
choices.why: That one stops new projects getting the default network.

choices.text: `iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts`
choices.why: A real constraint, about the role default service accounts receive; not the one the lesson names for keys.

prompt: Match each provider to the identity a program uses with no stored secret.
hint: The left column of the last table.

prompt: On Azure, a storage account allows anonymous access, but every container is set to private. What can a stranger read?
hint: Two switches have to be set.

choices.text: Every blob in the account
choices.why: The account switch alone exposes nothing; a container has to opt in too.

choices.text: The list of containers, but no blob inside them
choices.why: With every container private, anonymous requests get nothing at all.

choices.text: Only blobs uploaded after the account setting changed
choices.why: Upload time plays no part; the container's level decides.

choices.text: Nothing, until one container opts in as well
choices.why: Right. Azure's path needs both switches.

prompt: An Azure SAS signed with the storage account's key, and not tied to a stored access policy, has leaked. What does Microsoft's documentation offer?
hint: It has no revoke button of its own.

choices.text: Rotate the account's key, ending every such link at once
choices.why: Right. Blunt, and the reason a user delegation SAS is the recommended kind.

choices.text: Revoke that one SAS from the portal
choices.why: There is no per-SAS revoke for an ad hoc SAS.

choices.text: Nothing: wait for it to expire, since every SAS lasts at most an hour
choices.why: Its expiry is whatever its creator chose.

choices.text: Delete the blob, then upload it again under the same name
choices.why: The SAS is signed for the name, not for the upload, so it would read the new blob too.

prompt: The clinic switches its S3 bucket from the provider's default key to a customer-managed KMS key. What changed, according to the lesson?
hint: The disk was encrypted before as well.

choices.text: The data is now encrypted at rest, which it was not before
choices.why: Encryption at rest is on by default at all three providers.

choices.text: Nothing at all, since both keys belong to AWS in the end
choices.why: The customer-managed key has a key policy the clinic writes; that is the difference.

choices.text: Anyone with s3:GetObject can now read the files without a key
choices.why: The opposite direction: reading now also needs the key's permission.

choices.text: Who can switch the data off, and who sees each use of the key
choices.why: Right. Lesson 11 makes that concrete.

prompt: An Azure Key Vault still uses vault access policies, and the team reviews only Azure RBAC. What does the review miss?
hint: Two models, two lists.

choices.text: The keys' rotation dates
choices.why: Rotation is a property of keys, not of who reads them.

choices.text: Nothing, because access policies were retired from Azure and every vault moved to RBAC
choices.why: They still exist; the lesson calls them the older model.

choices.text: A second list of who reads secrets, in the vault's access policies
choices.why: Right. Microsoft recommends RBAC so there is one list.

choices.text: The vault's region, which RBAC hides
choices.why: RBAC hides no region; the gap is about who has access.

prompt: A virtual machine with a public address is launched in a Google Cloud project's `default` network, with no firewall rule written. Does SSH from the internet reach it?
hint: Read the default network's pre-made rules.

choices.text: Yes, through `default-allow-ssh`, which admits port 22 from `0.0.0.0/0`
choices.why: Right. Which is why Google advises deleting the default network in production.

choices.text: No: Google Cloud denies all ingress by default, in every network, until a rule allows it
choices.why: The implied rule does, but the default network adds rules above it, including SSH from anywhere.

choices.text: Only from other Google Cloud projects
choices.why: The rule's source is the whole internet.

choices.text: Only after the instance's service account is granted a role that allows SSH logins
choices.why: Network reachability is a firewall question; the service account plays no part in it.

prompt: Which of these are recorded by default, with nobody having configured anything? Choose all that apply.
hint: The middle column of the logs table is the one that is off.

choices.text: AWS management events, in CloudTrail's event history
choices.why: Right, for 90 days.

choices.text: Reads of objects in an S3 bucket
choices.why: Data events: off until a trail records them, and billed.

choices.text: Google Cloud's Admin Activity audit logs
choices.why: Right. Always on, and impossible to turn off.

choices.text: Google Cloud's Data Access audit logs for Cloud Storage
choices.why: Off by default; BigQuery is the exception.

choices.text: Azure's Activity Log for a subscription
choices.why: Right, for 90 days.

prompt: For how many days does Google Cloud keep Admin Activity audit logs in the `_Required` bucket?
hint: The logs table, last column.

prompt: After an incident, the clinic asks two questions of the AWS account: who changed the bucket's policy, and who read the patients' file. Nobody configured logging beforehand. What can be answered?
hint: One is a management event and one is a data event.

choices.text: Both, from CloudTrail's event history
choices.why: Event history holds management events only; object reads are data events.

choices.text: Only the first one, and only if it happened within 90 days
choices.why: Right. The middle column is the one that hurts after an incident.

choices.text: Neither, since no trail was created
choices.why: Event history records management events without a trail, for 90 days.

choices.text: The second, from the bucket's own access history
choices.why: A bucket keeps no access history unless logging was set up.

prompt: In the lab, `get-public-access-block` on the new `clinic-records` bucket answered `NoSuchPublicAccessBlockConfiguration`. What would AWS have answered?
hint: A default since April 2023.

choices.text: The same error, since new buckets have no configuration
choices.why: That is moto. AWS switches all four settings on for new buckets.

choices.text: All four settings, already true
choices.why: Right. Said from AWS's documentation, not run.

choices.text: An AccessDenied error, because reading the setting needs a separate permission
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests a refusal; the question is what the setting holds.

choices.text: Only BlockPublicPolicy set, with the other three left off
choices.why: AWS turns on all four together.

prompt: Why did `aws s3control put-public-access-block` never reach moto?
hint: Read the address in the error.

choices.text: moto refuses account-level settings with AccessDenied
choices.why: No answer came back at all; the request never connected.

choices.text: Account-level settings need the root user's password, which the lab never sets
choices.why: They need a permission, not the root user; and the error was a connection failure.

choices.text: The `test` key is not allowed to call S3 Control
choices.why: moto had no checking on in this section, and the request never arrived.

choices.text: The account number became part of a host name nothing resolves
choices.why: Right. On AWS the same pattern reaches the account's S3 Control endpoint.

prompt: The clinic's sentence is enforced by Azure Policy on a management group, by an Organization Policy constraint on the Google Cloud organisation, and by an SCP on the AWS root. Which part of its estate is outside all three?
hint: Three places, three ways to be exempt.

choices.text: Nothing, since each guardrail sits at its hierarchy's top
choices.why: The AWS one, at the root, still misses one account.

choices.text: The Google Cloud projects, since constraints apply to folders only
choices.why: A constraint on the organisation is inherited by every folder and project.

choices.text: The AWS management account, which no SCP reaches
choices.why: Right. The audit of the sentence has to visit it by other means.

choices.text: Azure subscriptions created after the policy was assigned
choices.why: A policy on a management group reaches subscriptions placed under it, new or old.

prompt: Order the levels of Azure's hierarchy from the top down.
hint: The figure's middle column.
trap: Putting the resource group above the subscription is the usual slip: a resource group lives inside one subscription.
